lines: A producer renames a column on an ordinary Tuesday, with every one of their own tests passing green.
Nothing in their own pipeline ever reads that old name, so from where they're sitting, nothing looks wrong at all.
Three other teams' dashboards, which do read it, find out only once they break in production, with no warning at all.
The identical rename, attempted against a real written contract instead, is rejected in minutes, naming all three owners by name.
Worth sitting with this question before the next few steps settle it directly.
The previous topic's write-audit-publish proves a pipeline's own deploy won't corrupt its own production table.
Does that exact same guarantee also protect every team that actually reads what that pipeline produces?
Or is protecting the publish itself a genuinely different problem from protecting the people downstream of it?
steps.answer: No, it's a different problem. A CI gate only enforces whatever its own tests happen to check. Nothing protects a downstream reader at all, unless something states, in a form a machine can actually check, exactly what the producer is promising them.

lines: Here's that something, built as one real, versioned, machine-readable file.
A table's schema lives right alongside its own quality rules, its service-level targets, and who actually owns it.
All four pieces sit together in one place, rather than scattered across four different documents nobody keeps in sync.
This one is built for real, for the shop's own orders table, following the actual published standard.
Now the gate that actually reads this contract before anything merges.
A straight rename, with nothing in the new schema naming what it replaces, gets classified as breaking with no path at all.
That exact classification is what blocks the merge outright, before the change ever reaches production.
The identical rename, proposed only once a replacement column openly names what it deprecates, is correctly let through instead.
steps.takeaway: A CI gate that reads the contract blocks exactly the renames a consumer never saw coming.

lines: One more question worth predicting before the next reveal answers it outright.
A CI gate only ever runs once a change actually goes through a real pull request, start to finish.
Does that cover every single way this contract could end up genuinely violated in practice?
Or is there a real kind of write that a pull-request-shaped gate could never see coming at all?
steps.answer: No, it doesn't cover every case. A write from an out-of-band job, run completely outside the normal pipeline, never goes through a pull request at all, so a CI gate never gets the chance to run against it in the first place.

lines: Here's exactly that case, caught by a second, completely separate check.
An out-of-band job writes straight to the table, skipping every pull request and every CI run entirely.
The same written contract, checked again for real at the actual moment of the write itself, is the only thing watching.
It catches a genuinely missing required field and a genuinely negative amount, neither one ever seen by any CI gate.
One more real mechanism, aimed at a completely different moment of risk.
An approved, non-breaking change to the orders table still genuinely reaches three separate downstream tables.
Those three tables are owned, in this real example, by three genuinely different teams across the company.
A real lineage graph finds every single one of those three owners automatically, and notifies each one without being asked.
steps.takeaway: Nobody has to remember who reads a table once its lineage graph already knows.

lines: Pulling all four of these real mechanisms together now, for real.
A contract as code, a producer-side CI gate, a runtime check, and lineage-driven owner notification.
Each one closes a genuinely different gap a safe deploy, all on its own, still leaves wide open.
Together, they're what makes a pipeline unable to ship a change its own stated promises would reject.
steps.takeaway: A pipeline that cannot ship a change its own promises would reject protects everyone who reads it.

lines: One real run to close out this entire chapter, against the shop's own contract.
Propose the exact same rename twice: once with absolutely no migration path, and once done properly through expand first.
Run both proposals through the exact same real classifier and the exact same real CI gate.
Does the gate end up blocking both renames, or does only the one with no real path ever get blocked?
steps.answer: Only the one with no real migration path gets blocked. The straight rename is classified breaking with no path and stopped outright, while the expand-first rename names exactly what it deprecates, and the gate correctly lets it through.
